answer.exemplar: An accumulated area and its rate of change are two views of one quantity. If A of x is the integral of a continuous f from a fixed starting point up to x, then A prime of x equals f of x, because nudging x upward by a small amount adds a thin sliver of area whose height is essentially f of x and whose width is that increase, so the ratio of area gained to width added tends to the height. Differentiating the accumulated area therefore hands back the integrand at the same point, which is why an antiderivative and a definite integral are two answers to one question asked in opposite directions. A model answer must make the sliver argument, since announcing the theorem without it leaves the direction of the reasoning unexplained.

questions.explanation: A model answer has to show the mechanism, because the theorem is usually stated before the argument behind it is available. The accumulated-area definition is the right place to start, and the thin-sliver reasoning is what turns it into a derivative. Merely restating that the two halves are linked does not teach why, which is exactly what the explanation floor is there to catch.
questions.hint: Start from the accumulated area, then argue with a thin sliver added as x increases.
questions.learningObjective: explain what the fundamental theorem connects and why it holds

answer.exemplar: A two-sided limit is a single number that the function approaches however x gets close to the point, and approaching from the left and from the right are equally valid ways of getting close. If the left-hand limit is 5 and the right-hand limit is 3, no single number can be named as the limit, because points on the left demand 5 while points on the right demand 3, and a limit must be one value that works for every approach. Taking 3 because the right side was seen last, or 4 as an average, describes no actual behaviour, since the curve never settles at either height. What the graph has at that point is a jump discontinuity, and the two one-sided limits name the heights on either side of the jump. A model answer must make the one-value-for-every-approach point, since that is the whole content of the definition.

questions.explanation: A model answer must argue from the definition of a limit as one value valid for every approach, because that is what forces the two sides to agree. The failure modes worth naming are picking a side and averaging, since both invent a height the curve never takes. A model answer should also say what the graph does have instead, which is a jump, since the two one-sided limits are exactly the heights beside it.
questions.hint: A limit is one value that has to work for every way of approaching the point.
questions.learningObjective: explain why a two-sided limit requires the one-sided limits to agree

answer.exemplar: A set of vectors is linearly dependent when at least one of them can be written as a linear combination of the others, so the set carries redundancy and spans a space of smaller dimension than it has members. The consequence for a system is a count of choices. If a coefficient vector can be zeroed while the system stays satisfied, then whatever holds for that vector also holds for all of its scalar multiples, so any one solution generates infinitely many and no unique one can be recovered. Independence removes exactly that freedom: if the columns are independent the transformation they define is one to one, so the right-hand side has either a single preimage or none at all. A model answer must connect the redundancy to the failure of uniqueness rather than leaving dependence as a bare definition.

questions.explanation: A model answer must link the algebraic condition, one vector being a combination of the others, to the practical consequence, a failure of uniqueness in the system. Stopping at the definition teaches nothing about why dependence matters. The pairing with invertibility is what makes the idea stick, since independence of the columns is exactly the condition that a square matrix can be inverted.
questions.hint: Ask what redundancy in the vectors does to the number of solutions.
questions.learningObjective: explain how vector dependence affects the solution set of a system

answer.exemplar: The distinction turns on whether the graph can be repaired. For the given function, factoring the numerator as the quantity x minus 1 times the quantity x plus 1 shows the denominator's factor cancelling away, so the function equals x plus 1 everywhere except at 1, where it is undefined. The limit at 1 exists and equals 2, so the graph has a single hole and defining the value at 1 to be 2 would make the function continuous there; that is removable. An infinite discontinuity instead has a vanishing denominator with nothing to cancel, as in 1 over x minus 1, where the sign of the denominator flips across the point and the graph is sent to opposite infinities. No value at the point repairs that, so it is not removable, and a model answer must say so rather than only describing the hole.

questions.explanation: A model answer must do the factorisation, because the cancelling factor is the whole reason the first case is repairable and the contrast is not visible from the shape of the formula alone. It must also say what infinite means, a graph sent away with no cancelling factor, since that is what makes repair impossible. Stopping at a hole that can be filled, without the factorisation, does not show why this particular function has a hole.
questions.hint: Factor the numerator and ask whether the denominator's factor cancels away.
questions.learningObjective: explain why one discontinuity is repairable and another is not

questions.explanation: The product of the two matrices is the matrix with rows (2, 1) and (4, 3), since each entry pairs a row of the first matrix with a column of the second. Its determinant is 2 times 3 minus 1 times 4, which is 6 minus 4, giving 2. The multiplicativity of determinants confirms it from the other direction: the first determinant is minus 2, the second is minus 1, and their product is also 2.

questions.explanation: Differentiating 3x squared gives 6x and differentiating minus x gives minus 1, so the derivative is the quantity 6x minus 1, and at x equal to 2 that is 12 minus 1, which is 11. The linear term contributes a constant slope of minus 1; dropping it gives 12, and negating the whole result gives the third option. A small difference of the function itself agrees: the rise from 1.9999 to 2.0001 is 0.0022 across a run of 0.0002, which is 11.

questions.explanation: Doubling the first row gives 4x plus 6y equals 26, exactly the second row, so subtracting the doubled first row from the second leaves a row reading 0 equals 0. That row is not a contradiction but a tautology, and it signals one free variable with infinitely many solutions rather than no solution. No solution would need a row reading 0 equals a nonzero constant, which is not what appears here, and the single surviving pivot leaves one of the two unknowns free.
questions.hint: Read the final row: 0 equals 0 is consistent, while 0 equals a nonzero constant is not.

questions.explanation: An antiderivative is x minus x squared, which at 3 is minus 6 and at 0 is 0, so the definite integral is minus 6. The curve crosses the axis where 1 minus 2x is 0, at x equal to 0.5, and below that it is negative across almost the whole interval, so the signed value is not the geometric area. That area would be 6, the magnitude, obtained by adding absolute areas rather than signed ones, and the negative sign is precisely the information that the curve spends most of its length below the axis.
